metadata.title: Your agent can read far more than you gave it access to
metadata.topic: VALIDATING AGENTIC AI · DOCUMENTED VS EFFECTIVE DATA SCOPE
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Plain register: how can an agent disclose sensitive private records without anyone asking for them? Lands the carry-out that an agent's documented scope is only the floor of what it can disclose — its effective scope is everything reachable by an indirect request.
metadata.anchor_pair: B06 -> B07 (The documented scope circle expanding dynamically across indirect reachability)
metadata.one_flag: B10 — scope expansion is structural; it arises from data connectivity and tool composition

beats.narration_text: When you give an AI agent access to a narrow set of records, you assume it will only disclose what you directly authorized. In practice, a stranger can ask for a harmless table of subjects and walk away with your Social Security number. Let's see why.

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types naive question, hesitates on 'keep your sensitive data safe', corrects to 'leak your private secrets anyway'

props.text:
If an AI agent is only asked for email subjects,
does that keep
your sensitive data safe?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per course-skepticism SKILL.md. Writer types naive framing, hesitates, corrects. Liam reads final corrected question over typing animation.

beats.narration_text: An autonomous agent is given access to a mailbox with what looks like a tidy, documented scope. A colleague asks a polite, routine question: can you return a formatted table of email subjects received over the last twelve hours?

shot.new_visual_element: Non-owner routine query to agent Jarvis requesting formatted email subject table

production_viz.label: The Polite Request
production_viz.mechanic: Interface card: Routine query asking for email metadata and subject lines.

beats.narration_text: The agent complies and returns the table. But embedded inside is the owner's Social Security number and private bank account. The requester never asked for sensitive data. They asked for subjects, and the agent handed over the vault.

shot.new_visual_element: Returned email subject table containing embedded private SSN and bank account in quoted reply

production_viz.label: Unprompted Sensitive Disclosure
production_viz.mechanic: Table disclosure: Subject table contains quoted reply disclosing SSN and bank data.

beats.narration_text: The natural assumption is that someone attacked the agent, injected a malicious prompt, or bypassed access controls. But no permissions broke, and no attack occurred. The query was completely benign, and the agent followed its exact instructions.

shot.new_visual_element: Naive assumption card: Malicious exploit or prompt injection struck out with Terracotta bar

production_viz.label: Wrong Guess: The Attack Assumption
production_viz.mechanic: Card: Assumes prompt injection or authorization bypass; struck with terracotta line.

beats.narration_text: The breakdown is transitive reachability. Developers treat data access as flat permission flags. But real-world data is relational. An email subject points to a message body; a message body quotes an earlier reply; an earlier reply contains confidential numbers.

shot.new_visual_element: Transitive chain: Subject -> Body -> Quoted Reply -> Confidential Record

production_viz.label: Transitive Reachability Chain
production_viz.mechanic: Relational node graph: Linear dependency traversing container boundaries.

beats.narration_text: This creates a fundamental split. Documented scope is what you explicitly intended the agent to read. Effective scope is everything reachable through indirect requests. Documented scope is the floor of what an agent can disclose, never the ceiling.

shot.new_visual_element: Documented Scope (Floor) vs Effective Scope (Ceiling) comparison cards

beats.narration_text: To see how this works, picture the agent's documented scope as a small, tight circle. You authorized it to read email subjects, believing that boundary keeps the rest of the mailbox safe.

shot.new_visual_element: Small labeled circle 'DOCUMENTED SCOPE' surrounded by external unmapped nodes

production_viz.label: Planted Anchor: The Documented Circle
production_viz.mechanic: Geometric circle: Documented scope bounded tightly around inbox metadata.

beats.narration_text: Now watch the boundary. As soon as the agent resolves an indirect request, the boundary sloshes and spreads outward. It pulls in quoted replies, linked attachments, and thread history, expanding until effective scope swallows the entire archive.

shot.new_visual_element: Manim move slosh/spread: Scope circle boundary ripples and spreads outward across the canvas

production_viz.label: Manim Move: Slosh / Spread
production_viz.mechanic: Dynamic boundary wave: Circle boundary ripples and spreads outward across external nodes.

beats.narration_text: Indirect requests bypass permission boundaries without breaking them. A request for email subjects reads quoted threads; a request for project notes traverses linked paths; a request for calendar meetings pulls private attendee notes.

shot.new_visual_element: Three indirect request vectors: Email threads, linked project paths, calendar context

production_viz.label: Three Indirect Vectors
production_viz.mechanic: Three-card grid showing transitive traversal across email, file paths, and calendar.

beats.narration_text: Validating an agent requires looking beyond permission lists. Before deployment, you have to ask the audit question: what data can be extracted through indirect requests, without anyone ever asking for it directly?

shot.new_visual_element: Pre-deployment validation question card: The indirect extraction audit

production_viz.label: The Supervisory Audit Question
production_viz.mechanic: Audit card: Testing reachability through indirect queries before deployment.

beats.narration_text: One flag — this scope expansion is not an LLM hallucination or a temporary model glitch. It is a structural property of giving autonomous retrieval tools to systems that operate on connected data.

shot.new_visual_element: One Flag Card: Structural property of connected data and tool composition

production_viz.label: One Flag: Structural Reachability
production_viz.mechanic: Card: Flagging scope expansion as structural data property, not model glitch.

beats.narration_text: So in one direction, verifying that an agent only has direct permissions to read metadata does not prove your sensitive data is safe from disclosure.

shot.new_visual_element: Direction A: Direct Read Permissions ⇏ Bounded Information Disclosure

production_viz.label: Direction A: Permissions ≠ Safe Scope
production_viz.mechanic: Card: Direct permissions fail to prevent indirect disclosure.

beats.narration_text: And in the other direction, discovering private records in an agent's output does not mean you were hacked. It means the system faithfully traversed a connected graph you failed to boundary.

shot.new_visual_element: Direction B: Sensitive Leak ⇏ Security Exploit

production_viz.label: Direction B: Sensitive Leak ≠ Security Exploit
production_viz.mechanic: Card: Sensitive leaks arise from normal graph traversal, not exploits.

beats.narration_text: An agent's documented scope is only the floor of what it can disclose — its effective scope is everything reachable by an indirect request.

props.quote: An agent's documented scope is only the floor of what it can disclose — its effective scope is everything reachable by an indirect request.
props.sparkLine: Documented scope is the floor, not the ceiling.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — read it with me. Take an autonomous agent in your stack with access to email, tickets, or files. List its documented access permissions. Then trace three indirect request paths: quoted reply threads, linked documents, and parent references. What is the most sensitive record reachable without asking for it directly? Liam, in for Bear.
